subject: Slight inconsistency with error checking in probability distributions.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Slight inconsistency with error checking in probability distributions.
parts:
When we calculate a log pdf up to a proportion, if all of arguments
are double, we return 0 without further checking.

If any of these values are agrad::var, we could end up throwing a
bounds error if the parameter value is invalid (even if it's double).

Should we change this behavior?

For example:
<code>
using stan::agrad::var

normal_log<true>(0, 0, -1); // no exception
normal_log<true>(var(0), 0, -1); // exception -- sd is < 0
</code>

Using generated code, this situation shouldn't arise, but users using
the C++ library directly could come across this.





Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Slight inconsistency with error checking in probability distributions.
parts:
On 9/17/12 1:58 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> When we calculate a log pdf up to a proportion, if all of arguments
> are double, we return 0 without further checking.
>
> If any of these values are agrad::var, we could end up throwing a
> bounds error if the parameter value is invalid (even if it's double).
>
> Should we change this behavior?

I don't think it's a big deal, but I do think it's worth
changing them so that double/var behave the same way for
consistency. It's easier to doc and test and easier for
users to debug that way.

I think it will change the models a bit because now

0 ~ normal(0,-1);

would throw a domain error in the model.

- Bob

> I don't think it's a big deal, but I do think it's worth
> changing them so that double/var behave the same way for
> consistency. It's easier to doc and test and easier for

Ok. I agree that it's easier conceptually when errors are thrown
consistently with double/var.

> I think it will change the models a bit because now
>
> 0 ~ normal(0,-1);
>
> would throw a domain error in the model.

Yes, that's true, but that statement just looks like there was a
mistake. This should still work:
0 ~ normal(0, 1);
